articles.title: Nearly 500 Africans recruited into Russia’s army have died, Ukraine says
articles.body:
486 Africans recruited into Russia’s armed forces are dead, while Ukraine is holding 35 citizens from 17 African countries as prisoners of war, Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) told Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne in findings published on 16 August 2026. Its overall tally rose only slightly from May, climbing from 2,965 recruits from 36 countries to at least 2,982 from 37.
Russia’s recruitment in Africa is part of a broader effort to enlist foreigners for its war. A joint human-rights investigation found that Russia had recruited at least 27,000 people from more than 130 countries since 2022. The system helps Moscow replenish its forces while shifting battlefield risk onto foreigners, many of whom are drawn in by financial pressure, deception, or coercion.
The largest groups of recruits came from Kenya, Egypt, Cameroon, Ghana, Nigeria, Uganda, Algeria, and Mali, the ministry told Suspilne.
Russia’s wider recruitment pipeline in Africa
Russian security services use a “broad arsenal of manipulative methods,” the Ukrainian MFA said. Recruiters promise civilian jobs, education, high salaries, Russian citizenship, or migration benefits. In many cases, foreigners must sign Russian-language military contracts under threat of deportation or imprisonment.
The FIDH–Truth Hounds–KIBHR report found recruiters using social media and intermediaries to advertise civilian jobs. Of 16 foreign POWs interviewed, 13 said they had been promised they would not fight. Most reached combat positions within weeks.
The human toll on African recruits
Kenyan engineer Francis told journalist Dmytro Karpenko, who interviews prisoners captured while fighting for Russia, that he thought he had accepted a security job. In Russia, he received a military uniform instead. After two weeks of training, he reached the front and was captured.
Nigerian recruits Hamzat Kazeen Kolawole and Mbah Stephen Udoka died in an assault after receiving little or no training, Ukrainian military intelligence said. Botswana reported “heartbreaking calls” from its citizens describing “perilous conditions” at the front.
Ukraine’s response to Russia's recruitment campaign
Ukraine’s diplomatic missions regularly inform African officials about the recruitment of their citizens and run awareness campaigns, according to the ministry.
The MFA and Ukraine’s POW Coordination Headquarters also launched Stop Russian Recruiters, a website that explains recruitment methods, shares victims’ accounts, advises people at risk and their families, and accepts reports about recruiters.

articles.title: Cairo talks expose growing gaps on Hamas's future in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Cairo talks expose deepening gaps over Hamas's future in Gaza
The recent Cairo talks between Hamas and US officials, notable US president DonaldTrump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, have exposed a widening gap over the movement's future in Gaza, with Washington demanding an end to its military role while Hamas seeks a political path that would allow it to remain part of the Palestinian system.
On Sunday, US envoy Kushner held a rare direct meeting with Hamas political bureau chief Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt.
The meeting was attended by Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish officials, as well as US envoy Nikolay Mladenov and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, as Washington seeks to revive its 15-point roadmap and advance negotiations towards a second phase which Israel has publicly rejected.
The talks focused on the most difficult issue facing the process: what happens to Hamas and its weapons.
According to Israeli media outlets, Kushner told Hamas that the Trump administration wanted to pursue a political path involving Palestinians, but that the movement first needed to dismantle its military capabilities, transfer control of Gaza to a Palestinian government and refrain from interfering in its administration.
Hamas, for its part, has linked any move on its weapons to Israeli steps, including an end to its daily deadly attacks that has killed over 1,400 people since the ceasefire, and a guarantee of an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza.
Preserving a political role
In a press statement on Monday, Hamas has indicated that it could transfer responsibility for Gaza to a Palestinian government and participate in future elections, but it has not agreed to surrender its weapons without guarantees over Israel's actions.
"Hamas's statement was careful, not mentioning Kushner directly, hinting at sensitive contacts," Gaza-based political analyst Taysir Abdullah told The New Arab.
Abdullah said Hamas appeared keen to maintain a relationship with the Trump administration, with Qatar and Turkey helping facilitate that channel. But he cautioned against interpreting the Cairo meeting as an agreement.
One of Washington's messages, according to hims, was that Hamas should not base its calculations on Israeli elections or wait for a possible change in government.
"Hamas is playing for time," Abdullah said, adding that the movement could be hoping for political changes in Israel that might create space for its continued involvement.
Political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim offered a more pessimistic assessment of Hamas's calculations.
He told TNA that the movement still appeared to be relying on time and political developments, including the possibility of participating in future Palestinian elections with international or US guarantees.
But Ibrahim argued that the reality on the ground was moving in the opposite direction.
The United States and Israel, he said, appeared determined to prevent Hamas from retaining the role it had before the war, particularly its military presence in Gaza.
Hamas may therefore be trying to preserve a political foothold, but the conditions being imposed by Washington and Israel make its return to the previous political arrangement increasingly unlikely, Ibrahim said.
Disarmament
The Trump administration's roadmap places disarmament at the centre of its proposed transition in Gaza. Other elements include an end to military operations, Israeli withdrawal, the transfer of administration to Palestinians, reconstruction and the deployment of an international stabilisation force.
Israeli media reported that Kushner made clear that Hamas's disarmament could not be indefinitely postponed.
Washington has also indicated that it could help guarantee Israeli commitments if Hamas takes concrete steps towards dismantling its military capabilities.
Political analyst Akram Atallah told TNA that the direct contact between Kushner and Hamas's leadership was important but came too late.
The meeting "should have happened a long time ago to stop the bloodshed of Palestinians," Atallah said.
He warned, however, against reading the talks as evidence of a fundamental change in US policy towards Hamas.
"The United States and Israel do not appear prepared to accept Hamas continuing with the same strength and in the same form as before the war," he said.
Atallah linked the pressure on Hamas to wider regional changes and efforts to establish a new political and security order in the Middle East, which have further reduced the movement's room for manoeuvre.
Hamas could seek to participate in future elections and secure US guarantees for that participation, he said, but added that "the regional and international reality is different."
"Israel and the United States are pushing for an end to Hamas's military presence in Gaza," Atallah added.
Balancing act
Washington's approach faced stiff resistance from Israel.
Kushner, Mladenov and Blair are expected to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss measures Israel would be expected to take alongside progress on Hamas's disarmament.
According to US sources, Israel is particularly concerned about Washington's reported demand to halt targeted killings of Hamas members, amid Israeli claims that the movement is attempting to rebuild its military capabilities.
Netanyahu's Likud party has also rejected criticism from Arab and Islamic countries over Israel's position on the Trump plan, accusing them of seeking to weaken the Israeli prime minister and force concessions.
The disagreement means that even if Hamas were to move towards disarmament, questions would remain over what Israel would be prepared to offer in return.
For Hamas, giving up its weapons without a clear Israeli withdrawal could eliminate its remaining leverage. For Israel and Washington, allowing the movement to retain its military capabilities while entering the political process would conflict with their vision for post-war Gaza.
Egypt has emerged as a key actor in efforts to keep the negotiations moving. Kushner also met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, who, according to sources, stressed the importance of adhering to the ceasefire agreement.
One source familiar with the meetings said Sisi argued that the Gaza war had contributed to wider regional instability and that restoring calm in the Strip would have consequences beyond Gaza.
Egypt, Qatar and Turkey are now working with Washington to prevent the process from stalling before the second phase can begin.
For Cairo, the stakes also include humanitarian aid and reconstruction, both of which could be delayed by a prolonged political deadlock.
But the Cairo meetings have not resolved the central disagreement.
Hamas is seeking a political future and wants guarantees before giving up its weapons. Washington and Israel are seeking to dismantle its military structure before allowing it a meaningful role in the post-war order.
The three analysts differ in emphasis, but their assessments point to the same broader problem: Hamas may still be calculating that time and political change can preserve its position, while the conditions being set by Israel and the United States are designed to prevent a return to the pre-war status quo.
The Kushner-Hayya meeting therefore represents an important channel of communication, but not a breakthrough.
The question now is whether Cairo can generate sufficient momentum on both sides to keep the ceasefire process alive or whether the dispute over Hamas's future will prevent the negotiations from reaching their next stage.

South Korea Fires Warning Shots After North Korean Troops Cross the DMZ
South Korean troops fired warning shots after a group of North Korean soldiers crossed the Military Demarcation Line separating the two countries, Yonhap reported on August 16.
The incident occurred last week along the eastern section of the heavily fortified border, where several North Korean troops briefly crossed the line into South Korean-controlled territory.

According to the report, the soldiers were likely conducting a patrol in the area. South Korean forces issued warnings before firing warning shots, after which the North Korean troops returned to their side of the border.
Under South Korea’s current rules of engagement, troops first broadcast warnings when North Korean personnel approach or cross the Military Demarcation Line. If the violation continues, South Korean forces may fire warning shots.
The incident is the latest in a growing series of brief border crossings as North Korea intensifies construction and fortification work along the frontier.
North Korean troops crossed the demarcation line 17 times last year, according to South Korean military data.
Previously, reports emerged that South Korea would refrain from providing lethal military aid to Ukraine despite deepening military alignment between Pyongyang and Moscow.

articles.title: Russia Is Paying Five Times More for Every Dollar Ukraine Spends on Strikes
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Is Paying Five Times More for Every Dollar Ukraine Spends on Strikes
Ukraine’s Armed Forces are inflicting losses on Russia worth several times more than the cost of the weapons used to cause them, according to data tracked by the Mission Control module of Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system, the Ministry of Defense reported on August 17.
The numbers offer a detailed look at the economics of Ukraine’s battlefield strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Mission Control data for June, every $1 Ukraine spent on engaging Russian targets produced approximately $5 in estimated losses for Russia.
Mission Control was launched six months ago and has rapidly become a major source of battlefield data for Ukrainian commanders.
The system now processes around 50,000 combat missions every week, along with more than 230,000 reports documenting their results.
Every mission is recorded, allowing Ukrainian units to examine whether an operation succeeded, identify what worked and what failed, determine why, and adjust tactics for future missions.
The system also calculates how much Ukraine spends, on average, to engage different types of targets.
In June, the average cost was approximately $3,032 per Russian servicemember targeted, $2,674 per piece of military equipment, and $1,487 per infrastructure target, according to the Defense Ministry.
For comparison, Mission Control estimates that sustaining a single Russian servicemember costs Moscow approximately $65,000.
That cost disparity is particularly important for Ukraine, which is increasingly trying to maximize the battlefield effect of relatively inexpensive drones, precision weapons, and other strike systems against higher-value Russian personnel, equipment, and infrastructure.
Mission Control does more than calculate the cost of individual strikes.
The system categorizes missions by purpose, including reconnaissance, strikes, logistics, and evacuation. It also tracks how deep units operate, including missions conducted beyond 20 kilometers and 50 kilometers from the front.
Commanders can examine which weapons and systems individual units are using, how effectively they are employing them, and how much each successful engagement costs.
The platform separately records Ukrainian equipment losses, allowing military planners to determine the conditions and distances at which vehicles, drones, and other systems are most likely to be lost.
That creates a feedback loop in which battlefield performance can be measured not only by whether a target was hit, but by how much it cost, which weapon worked best, how far from the front it was used, and what Ukraine lost in the process.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says the growing pool of data allows units to adapt faster as battlefield conditions change and improve the efficiency of future combat missions.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia suffered nearly 43,000 battlefield casualties in July 2026, making it the Russian military’s highest monthly loss figure since January 2025, while Ukrainian forces recorded their largest territorial gains in more than a year.

articles.title: Russia’s most-used map app is erasing a Baltic missile site that Western maps still show
articles.body:
Russia's most-used mapping service has digitally hidden a military missile site near Finland by copying a fake forest over it on satellite imagery, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported. Western map services still show the same position, and a Finnish military analyst called the concealment careless and self-defeating. The clumsy edit points to Moscow's growing fear of Ukrainian drones.
What Yandex tried to erase
The concealed site sits beside the Kronstadt naval base, on Kotlin Island off St. Petersburg in the Gulf of Finland. Editing software copied trees from another image and laid them over the missile position. Until now, Russia mostly blurred sensitive locations rather than deleting them, but this edit tries to hide the target's existence outright. The same battery still appears on Google, Apple, and Microsoft satellite maps. In the covered zone, Russia has previously kept Bastion anti-ship missiles and their radar and reconnaissance systems.
A cover-up that gives itself away
Marko Eklund, a military expert and former Finnish intelligence officer, called the secrecy pointless. Western and Ukrainian analysts read their own satellite images, not Yandex, so the edit protects nothing in practice. He believes an administrative order drove it, and that the work was done sloppily. Anyone who knows what to look for can spot the seams and repeating patterns.

A pattern set by Ukraine's drones
Russia's map cover-ups have tracked Ukraine's deep strikes. A Moscow court ordered Yandex to mask an oil refinery in Ryazan in 2024 after repeated Ukrainian strikes, and a Nordic-Baltic investigation later counted 119 blurred sites near Russia's northwestern border. Blurring shows up at once, while cloned forest hides the tampering itself.
Kronstadt gives Russia one of its main Baltic Fleet bases, and Ukraine's drones have already reached it. In early June, they set a Russian missile corvette ablaze in dry dock there.

articles.title: Russia cancels major Red Square military jamboree amid drone attacks
articles.body:
A major military music festival in Moscow has been canceled four days before it was due to start, the organizers said on Telegram.
The lavish parade, known as the Spasskaya Tower International Military Music Festival, attracts thousands of visitors and brings together dozens of military bands in the heart of Moscow on Red Square near the Kremlin.
The event, which began in 2007 at President Vladimir Putin’s orders, is one of Russia’s most prominent military-themed events, alongside the May 9 Victory Day parade in Moscow and the Navy Day show in St. Petersburg. Spasskaya “Tower was only canceled once before — in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Advertisement
In its early years, military bands from EU countries, Australia and Canada took part in Spasskaya Tower, though the number of international participants has declined since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
According to the festival’s Telegram channel, “the event has been postponed until 2027 due to circumstances beyond the organizers’ control.”
The move comes amid an increase in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Russian capital.
Overnight, Kyiv’s forces launched one of the largest assaults on Moscow in recent months, with more than 600 drones directed toward the Russian capital and surrounding region. The strikes, which, according to Russian media, targeted the facilities of Wildberries, a major Russian online marketplace, as well as logistics warehouses, sparked massive fires and killed one person.
Earlier in June, the Kremlin canceled another event in Moscow’s Red Square — a gala concert marking Russia Day. The Victory Day parade on May 9 was held on a limited scale and, for the first time in nearly 20 years, without heavy military equipment.
